displayQuote: Put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket

meta.title: Who really said "Put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Andrew Carnegie said it in an 1885 address to the Curry Commercial College, printed in The Empire of Business (1902). Mark Twain reused it in 1894.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified as Andrew Carnegie's, from his 1885 Curry Commercial College address printed in The Empire of Business (1902) — not Mark Twain's, though Twain reworked it.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Carnegie said it in “The Road to Business Success: A Talk to Young Men,” an address to students of the Curry Commercial College, Pittsburg, on 23 June 1885. The address was printed in his 1902 collection The Empire of Business, where page 17 carries the line word for word — including the “then” that most modern versions drop.

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: The Road to Business Success: A Talk to Young Men
Address to students of the Curry Commercial College, Pittsburg — June 23, 1885
The Yonkers Statesman (Yonkers, New York), August 19, 1885, under the title “Success in Business”
The Empire of Business (New York: Doubleday, Page & Co., 1902)
17 — exact wording confirmed in the scanned first edition

source.excerpt: And here is the prime condition of success, the great secret: concentrate your energy, thought, and capital exclusively upon the business in which you are engaged. … The concerns which fail are those which have scattered their capital, which means that they have scattered their brains also. They have investments in this, or that, or the other, here, there and everywhere. “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket” is all wrong. I tell you “put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket.” Look round you and take notice; men who do that do not often fail. It is easy to watch and carry the one basket. It is trying to carry too many baskets that breaks most eggs in this country.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its main sourced Quotes section for Carnegie, cited to a “Speech to Curry Commercial College of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 23 June 1885” — the pointer that tells you which book to open.

Quote Investigator ↗ ran the full trace and concludes Carnegie “deserves credit for the sayings he employed” in that 1885 address — it also logs contemporaneous newspaper printings of the speech from August 1885 on — with Mark Twain adopting and popularising the line afterwards.

The claim checks out against the book itself: the OCR of the 1902 Doubleday, Page & Co. edition ↗ carries the sentence verbatim on page 17, and the essay’s opening page footnotes the Curry Commercial College date.
The Twain trail runs separately: his own reworking appears as the Chapter XV epigraph in The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) ↗, attributed there to the fictional “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar.”
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1902 Doubleday, Page & Co. printing; the ellipsis skips one sentence of setup. Note the closing footnote on the essay’s opening page: “From an address to Students of the Curry Commercial College, Pittsburg, June 23, 1885.”

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: Andrew Carnegie
author.bio: Born in Dunfermline, Scotland in 1835 and raised in Pittsburgh after his family emigrated, Carnegie built Carnegie Steel into the largest integrated iron and steel operation ever owned by one man in the United States, then sold it to J. P. Morgan in 1901 in the deal that created U.S. Steel. He spent his last decades giving away roughly ninety percent of his fortune — some 3,000 public libraries, Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Mellon University. The eggs-in-one-basket line is pure Carnegie doctrine: he distrusted diversification and preached concentration as the single condition of business success.

misattribution.heading: Why Mark Twain keeps getting the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare cases where the famous name on the quote card is right and the other famous name is the interloper. Carnegie said it first; Mark Twain made it stick.

items.why: Twain put a version of the maxim in the mouth of his fictional almanac-writer as the epigraph to Chapter XV of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) ↗. Because that is a novel people actually read, the line travels under Twain’s name. Quote Investigator ↗ reports that Twain himself copied the saying into a notebook in 1893 and credited Carnegie with it.

Twain’s printed text reads “Put all your eggs in the one basket and—watch that basket” — the one basket, no “then,” and wrapped in a fool-versus-wise-man frame. If you are quoting the version with “and then watch that basket,” you are quoting Carnegie ↗, not Twain.

The line is often reprinted with no author at all, as though it were a traditional saying that has always existed alongside “don’t put all your eggs in one basket.” Quote Investigator ↗ notes an 1875 newspaper precursor playing on the same image, so the joke of inverting the proverb was in the air — but the specific two-clause maxim belongs to Carnegie’s 1885 talk.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is Carnegie’s own, on page 17 of The Empire of Business (1902) ↗: “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket” is all wrong. I tell you “put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket.”

context.heading: Why Carnegie said it
lead: The line is not a stray aphorism — it is the punchline of the one piece of advice Carnegie called “the prime condition of success, the great secret”: concentrate your energy, thought and capital on the single business you are in. He had just told the students that the firms which fail are the ones that scattered their capital, “which means that they have scattered their brains also.”

Then he did something rhetorically neat: he took the safest, most respectable proverb in commerce and flipped it. Diversification, to a man who had bet everything on steel and won, looked like a way of guaranteeing you would never watch anything closely enough.
context.detailsSummary: He liked it enough to say it twice
detailsBody: The address closes with a rapid-fire summary of Carnegie’s rules — aim for the highest, never enter a bar-room, never speculate, make the firm’s interest yours — and the basket maxim reappears in that list, compressed to “concentrate; put all your eggs in one basket, and watch that basket; expenditure always within revenue.”

The same doctrine surfaces elsewhere in The Empire of Business, where Carnegie writes that the proverb “does not apply to a man’s life work” and that putting all your eggs in one basket and then watching that basket “is the true doctrine.”
context.pull: It is trying to carry too many baskets that breaks most eggs in this country.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this saying, traces it to Andrew Carnegie's 23 June 1885 address at Curry Commercial College titled "The Road to Business Success: A Talk to Young Men" (reprinted in The Empire of Business, 1902), notes an 1875 New-York Tribune precursor, and reports Mark Twain recorded it in an 1893 notebook crediting Carnegie before using it in Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894).

The full text of The Empire of Business (1902) contains, on page 17 of "The Road to Business Success: A Talk to Young Men", the sentences: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket" is all wrong. I tell you "put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket." It also carries the footnote "From an address to Students of the Curry Commercial College, Pittsburg, June 23, 1885" and the copyright line "Copyright 1902 by Doubleday, Page & Co."
The Internet Archive item is The empire of business by Andrew Carnegie (1835-1919), published by Doubleday, Page & Co., New York, 1902, 374 pages.

Wikiquote's Andrew Carnegie page lists, in its main Quotes section,: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket" is all wrong. I tell you "put all your eggs in one basket, and then watch that basket." cited to Speech to Curry Commercial College of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 23 June 1885.

Chapter XV of The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson contains the epigraph: Behold, the fool saith, "Put not all thine eggs in the one basket"--which is but a manner of saying, "Scatter your money and your attention;" but the wise man saith, "Put all your eggs in the one basket and--watch that basket"--Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar.
Project Gutenberg ebook 102 is The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson by Mark Twain (1835-1910), an 1894 novel.
Wikiquote's Pudd'nhead Wilson page reproduces the Chapter 15 epigraph about putting all your eggs in the one basket and watching that basket.

Andrew Carnegie was born 25 November 1835 in Dunfermline, Fife, Scotland and died 11 August 1919 in Lenox, Massachusetts; he built Carnegie Steel and sold it to J. P. Morgan in 1901, then gave away roughly 90% of his fortune including funding around 3,000 public libraries.
